newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow City Telephone sees growth high but slowing.
newsitem.headline: Moscow City Telephone sees growth high but slowing.

text.p: One of Russia's biggest regional telecom companies, Moscow's MGTS, announced higher 1996 profits on Wednesday but said runaway growth would slow this year.
"It is going to be a slightly more difficult year than in 1996," MGTS chief executive Vladimir Lagutin told a news conference.
AO Moskovskaya Gorodskaya Telefonnaya Set (MGTS) said 1996 net profit rose to 345.9 billion roubles ($59.9 million) from 165.4 billion to Russian accruals accounting standards.
Lagutin said he expected sales to grow by only 17.9 percent in 1997, as opposed to about 80 percent -- from 1.27 trillion roubles to 2.31 trillion roubles -- in 1996.
He predicted pre-tax profit would rise 25 percent in 1997 on last year, against 70 percent growth in 1996.
Results for the first quarter of 1997 released later on Wednesday showed pre-tax profit rose to 145.1 billion roubles from 87.0 billion roubles in the first quarter of 1996.

Russia's regional telecoms companies are considered among the most promising sectors in the economy, but analysts have said diminishing rates of revenue growth due to declining or static rates and higher costs will break growth this year.
Local call metering planned by many telecoms will boost revenues in the long-term, but political resistance to what is seen as an unpopular measure is delaying implementation.
Lagutin said the company hoped to receive a rating in September for its planned $150 million Eurobond, which he said would be issued in the second half of the year.
Access to financing is also separating companies, raising the possibility that the few who raise funds on international markets would leap ahead with infrastructure building.
International long-distance provider Rostelekom also plans a Eurobond this year, although the issue volume has not been announced, and analysts expect the market to welcome the issues.
Lagutin said the two companies would unwrap a new, cheaper long-distance service this year.

"This year MGTS together with Rostelekom will offer its clients an alternative long-distance and international service with lower prices and significantly higher quality," Lagutin said, adding it would be offered in the second half of the year.
Lagutin said metering equipment would be installed by the end of the year but said the city government would decide when telephone metering would be implemented.
MGTS added 45,300 lines out of a planned 90,000 in 1996. Moscow telephones per resident are about three times the national average at 49.7 per 100, MGTS said.
